title: Plant Transport Systems
description: How water and nutrients move through plants — xylem, phloem, transpiration, translocation, and factors affecting water loss.

notes.heading: Why Do Plants Need Transport Systems?
notes.body: Unlike animals, plants do not have a heart to pump fluids. Instead, they rely on physical processes — evaporation, osmosis, and capillary action. Plants need two transport systems: (1) Xylem — transports water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots up to the leaves and stems (one direction: upward). (2) Phloem — transports dissolved sugars (mainly sucrose) and amino acids from where they are made (source — mainly leaves through photosynthesis) to where they are needed or stored (sink — roots, fruits, growing tips). This is called translocation and can move in either direction (up or down) depending on where the sugars are needed. These two vascular tissues are found together in vascular bundles (veins) running through the plant. In roots, xylem is in the centre (resists pulling forces); in stems, vascular bundles are arranged in a ring (dicots) or scattered (monocots). The movement of water through a plant — from soil, into roots, up through xylem, and out through leaves — is called the transpiration stream.

illustration.alt: Diagram of a plant showing xylem carrying water upward from roots to leaves and phloem carrying sugars between sources and sinks.
illustration.caption: Xylem moves water one-way from roots to leaves; phloem moves sugars two-way from source to sink.

notes.heading: Xylem: Structure and Function
notes.body: Xylem vessels are dead, hollow tubes formed from cells laid end-to-end. Their end walls have broken down, creating a continuous, uninterrupted tube from root to leaf. The cell walls are thickened and strengthened with lignin — a waterproof, rigid substance deposited in rings, spirals, or solid patterns. Lignin provides structural support (xylem helps hold the plant upright) and prevents the walls from collapsing under the negative pressure (tension) created during transpiration. Key features: (1) No cytoplasm, no nucleus, no organelles — hollow lumen maximises water flow. (2) Lignified walls — mechanical strength and waterproofing. (3) No end walls — continuous column of water. (4) Pits (gaps in lignin) — allow water to move sideways between adjacent xylem vessels and into surrounding tissues. Water moves through xylem by two mechanisms: (1) Root pressure — minerals actively transported into xylem lower water potential, drawing water in by osmosis. This is minor. (2) Transpiration pull — the main force. Water evaporates from leaf mesophyll cells → creates negative pressure (tension) → pulls the entire water column up through xylem (cohesion-tension theory). Water molecules stick together (cohesion) through hydrogen bonding, so the pull from the top is transmitted all the way down to the roots.

illustration.alt: Longitudinal view of a xylem vessel showing lignin rings, pits, hollow lumen, and upward water movement.
illustration.caption: Lignin strengthens xylem walls; pits allow sideways water movement; the hollow lumen lets water flow continuously upward.

notes.heading: Phloem: Structure and Translocation
notes.body: Phloem is composed of living cells: sieve tube elements and companion cells. Sieve tube elements — long, thin cells arranged end-to-end. Their end walls are perforated (sieve plates) allowing sugar solution to flow through. Unlike xylem, sieve tube elements ARE alive, but they have lost their nucleus and most organelles to reduce flow resistance. Companion cells — small cells adjacent to each sieve tube element. They retain their nucleus and many mitochondria, providing ATP energy to actively load sugars into the sieve tubes (using active transport). Translocation is the movement of dissolved sugars (sucrose) and amino acids from sources to sinks. Sources: mature leaves (photosynthesis), storage organs during mobilisation (e.g., potato tuber sprouting). Sinks: growing tips (meristems), developing fruits, roots, storage organs. The pressure-flow hypothesis explains movement: sugars are actively loaded into phloem at the source, lowering water potential → water enters by osmosis from xylem → high hydrostatic pressure at source. At the sink, sugars are removed (used or converted to starch), raising water potential → water leaves → low pressure. The pressure gradient drives bulk flow of phloem sap from source to sink.

illustration.alt: Diagram of phloem showing sieve tube elements, companion cells, sieve plates, and sugar flow from source to sink.
illustration.caption: Companion cells supply ATP to load sugars into sieve tubes; the pressure gradient drives sap from source to sink.

notes.heading: Transpiration: Water Loss from Leaves
notes.body: Transpiration is the evaporation of water vapour from the surfaces of mesophyll cells into the air spaces of the leaf, followed by diffusion out through the stomata. It is an unavoidable consequence of gas exchange — stomata must be open to allow CO₂ in for photosynthesis, which means water vapour can escape. Transpiration provides several benefits: (1) Cooling effect (evaporative cooling — like sweating). (2) Delivery of dissolved mineral ions from roots (they travel with the water). (3) Maintains turgor pressure in cells (keeps non-woody plants upright). The transpiration stream: water evaporates from mesophyll cells → water potential decreases in these cells → water moves from xylem into mesophyll by osmosis → tension pulls water up the xylem column → water enters roots from soil by osmosis. This is a passive process — no energy is expended by the plant directly on transpiration (unlike translocation, which requires ATP for phloem loading).

illustration.alt: Cross-section of a leaf showing water evaporating from mesophyll cells and diffusing out through stomata.
illustration.caption: Water evaporates from moist mesophyll cell walls, moves through air spaces, and exits via stomata.

notes.heading: Factors Affecting Transpiration Rate
notes.body: Four main environmental factors affect the rate of transpiration: (1) Light intensity — brighter light → stomata open wider for photosynthesis → more water vapour escapes. Rate increases with light intensity (up to a plateau). (2) Temperature — higher temperature → more kinetic energy → faster evaporation from mesophyll cells; also increases the water-holding capacity of air. Rate increases with temperature. (3) Air movement (wind) — moving air removes the humid layer of air that builds up around the stomata (the boundary layer), maintaining a steep water vapour concentration gradient → faster diffusion. Still air allows humidity to build up, slowing transpiration. (4) Humidity — high humidity (lots of water vapour in air) → shallow concentration gradient between leaf interior and exterior → slower transpiration. Low humidity (dry air) → steep gradient → fast transpiration. Measuring transpiration rate: a potometer measures water uptake by a cut shoot. As the shoot transpires, an air bubble moves along a capillary tube. Distance moved per unit time gives the rate (mm/min). Limitations: this measures water uptake, not transpiration directly (some water is used in photosynthesis, most is transpired). A potometer must be airtight and the shoot cut under water to prevent air entering xylem.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing how light intensity, temperature, wind, and humidity affect the rate of leaf transpiration.
illustration.caption: Light, temperature, and wind increase transpiration; high humidity slows it by reducing the diffusion gradient.

notes.heading: Stomata and Guard Cells: Regulating Water Loss
notes.body: Stomata (singular: stoma) are tiny pores, mainly on the lower epidermis of leaves, surrounded by a pair of guard cells. They are the gateway for gas exchange — CO₂ enters, O₂ and water vapour exit. Guard cells are kidney-shaped in dicots (most plants). They regulate stomatal opening: (1) During the day — guard cells photosynthesise (they contain chloroplasts) → produce ATP → ATP powers active transport of potassium ions (K⁺) into guard cells → water potential decreases → water enters by osmosis → guard cells swell and curve → stoma opens. (2) At night — K⁺ ions pumped out → water potential increases → water leaves → guard cells become flaccid → stoma closes. This minimises water loss when photosynthesis is not occurring. In hot, dry conditions, even during the day, stomata may partially close to conserve water (at the cost of reduced photosynthesis). Adaptations of xerophytes (plants adapted to dry habitats): sunken stomata (in pits — humid air trapped reduces water loss), rolled leaves (reduces exposed surface area), thick waxy cuticle, hairs on leaves (trap humid air), reduced leaf area (spines instead of leaves, e.g., cacti). Adaptations of hydrophytes (aquatic plants): stomata on upper surface only (lower surface submerged), reduced cuticle (water loss not a concern), large air spaces for buoyancy and oxygen transport.

illustration.alt: Comparison of open and closed stomata showing potassium ions and water moving into or out of guard cells.
illustration.caption: Day: K⁺ and water enter guard cells, making them turgid and opening the pore. Night: K⁺ and water leave, cells become flaccid and close.

notes.heading: Practical: Using a Potometer and Investigating Mineral Deficiencies
notes.body: A potometer is used to measure the rate of water uptake, which approximates transpiration rate. Method: (1) Cut a leafy shoot under water (prevents air bubbles entering xylem). (2) Insert the shoot into the potometer under water using a rubber bung — ensure an airtight seal (use Vaseline if needed). (3) Introduce an air bubble into the capillary tube. (4) Measure the distance the bubble moves in a set time (e.g., 5 minutes). (5) Reset and repeat under different conditions (e.g., varying light by changing lamp distance, varying wind using a fan, varying humidity by enclosing in a plastic bag). Calculate rate = distance moved ÷ time. Controlled variables: leaf surface area, temperature, humidity (when testing light). Important: the bubble must be returned to the start position between readings (open the reservoir tap). Mineral deficiency practical: grow plants (e.g., duckweed or seedlings) in water culture solutions, each lacking one specific mineral (nitrate, magnesium, potassium, phosphate). A control has the complete nutrient solution. After several weeks, compare growth and deficiency symptoms. This demonstrates that each mineral has a specific role and cannot be substituted.

illustration.alt: Diagram of a potometer with a leafy shoot and an air bubble, plus water-culture tubes for mineral deficiency tests.
illustration.caption: A potometer measures water uptake by tracking an air bubble; water cultures show the effect of missing minerals.

flashcards.definition: Dead, hollow tubes reinforced with lignin that transport water and dissolved minerals upwards from roots to leaves. Part of the transpiration stream.
flashcards.example: Water absorbed by root hair cells enters xylem and travels up to the leaves for photosynthesis.

flashcards.definition: Living tubes (sieve tube elements + companion cells) that transport dissolved sugars (sucrose) and amino acids bidirectionally — from sources to sinks (translocation).
flashcards.example: Phloem transports glucose produced in leaf photosynthesis down to potato tubers for storage as starch.

flashcards.definition: The evaporation of water vapour from mesophyll cells into leaf air spaces, followed by diffusion out through stomata. Creates the tension that pulls water up through xylem.
flashcards.example: A large oak tree can transpire over 500 litres of water on a hot, sunny day.

flashcards.definition: The active transport of dissolved sugars (sucrose) and amino acids through phloem from sources (leaves, storage organs) to sinks (growing tips, roots, fruits).
flashcards.example: In spring, starch stored in potato tubers is converted to sucrose and translocated up to growing shoots.

flashcards.definition: The continuous column of water moving from roots → xylem → leaves, driven by transpiration pull at the top and root pressure at the bottom.
flashcards.example: Cohesion between water molecules (hydrogen bonding) ensures the transpiration stream remains unbroken.

flashcards.definition: Microscopic pores, mainly on the underside of leaves, surrounded by guard cells. Open during the day for CO₂ entry; close at night to conserve water.
flashcards.example: In hot, dry conditions, guard cells lose turgor and stomata close — reducing photosynthesis but preventing lethal water loss.

flashcards.definition: A pair of kidney-shaped cells surrounding each stoma. They actively pump K⁺ ions to change turgor and open/close the pore.
flashcards.example: At dawn, guard cells pump in K⁺ → water follows by osmosis → cells swell and curve → stoma opens.

flashcards.definition: A tough, waterproof polymer deposited in xylem cell walls, providing structural support and preventing collapse under tension.
flashcards.example: The wood of trees is mainly xylem tissue thickened with lignin — this is why wood is strong and hard.

flashcards.definition: An apparatus measuring water uptake by a cut shoot. An air bubble in a capillary tube moves as water is taken up; rate = distance ÷ time (mm/min).
flashcards.example: A potometer can compare transpiration rates under different conditions — fan (wind), lamp (light), plastic bag (humidity).

flashcards.definition: A living but nucleus-free cell forming the main conducting vessel of phloem. End walls have sieve plates allowing phloem sap to flow through.
flashcards.example: Companion cells provide ATP and metabolic support to sieve tube elements, which have lost most of their own organelles.

flashcards.definition: A specialised epidermal cell with a long projection that massively increases surface area for absorbing water (by osmosis) and mineral ions (by active transport) from soil.
flashcards.example: A single rye plant has about 14 billion root hairs, providing a surface area roughly the size of a football pitch.

flashcards.definition: Explains water transport in xylem: transpiration at leaves creates tension (suction) that pulls water up; water molecules cohere (stick together via hydrogen bonds), so the whole column moves upward.
flashcards.example: This is why a tall redwood tree (over 100 m) can pull water from roots to top leaves — the cohesive strength of water is enormous.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between xylem and phloem?
choices: Xylem transports sugars; phloem transports water
Xylem is dead tissue transporting water and minerals upwards; phloem is living tissue transporting sugars bidirectionally
Xylem is in roots only; phloem is in leaves only
Xylem is living; phloem is dead
questions.explanation: Xylem is composed of dead, hollow, lignified cells carrying water up. Phloem is living (sieve tubes + companion cells), transporting sugars from sources to sinks in either direction.

questions.stem: What force primarily drives water up through the xylem of a tall tree?
choices: Root pressure pushing water upwards from below
Transpiration pull — evaporation from leaves creates tension that pulls the water column up
Capillary action alone
Gravity pulling water molecules upward
questions.explanation: Transpiration (water evaporation from leaves) creates negative pressure (tension) at the top of the xylem column. This tension, combined with cohesion between water molecules, pulls the entire column upward — the cohesion-tension theory.

questions.stem: On a hot, dry, windy day, a plant's transpiration rate will:
choices: Decrease because the plant conserves water
Increase — high temperature increases evaporation, wind removes humid air around stomata maintaining a steep diffusion gradient
Stay the same regardless of conditions
Stop completely
questions.explanation: High temperature increases the kinetic energy of water molecules (faster evaporation). Wind removes humid air from around stomata, keeping the water vapour concentration gradient steep, which speeds up diffusion.

questions.stem: Which vessel has lignin deposited in its walls and why?
choices: Phloem — lignin helps transport sugars faster
Xylem — lignin provides structural support and waterproofs the walls, preventing collapse under the tension created by transpiration
Both xylem and phloem — all transport vessels need lignin
Neither — lignin is only found in bark
questions.explanation: Xylem is strengthened with lignin rings/spirals. This prevents the thin-walled tubes from collapsing inward when transpiration creates negative pressure (suction) inside the vessel.

questions.stem: In a potometer, what does the movement of the air bubble actually measure?
choices: The exact rate of transpiration
The rate of water uptake by the cut shoot (which approximates transpiration rate — most water taken up IS transpired)
The rate of photosynthesis in the leaves
The rate of sugar translocation in phloem
questions.explanation: A potometer measures water uptake. A very small fraction (~1-2%) of the water is used in photosynthesis and cell expansion; the vast majority (~98-99%) is lost through transpiration. So water uptake closely approximates transpiration rate.

questions.stem: What happens to guard cells when they pump potassium ions (K⁺) in during the day?
choices: They become flaccid and the stoma closes
Water follows by osmosis, guard cells swell and curve, opening the stoma
They die — guard cells cannot survive K⁺ accumulation
Nothing — K⁺ movement has no effect on stomatal opening
questions.explanation: Active transport of K⁺ into guard cells lowers their water potential. Water enters by osmosis, making them turgid. Due to their uneven cell wall thickness, they curve, creating a pore — the open stoma.

questions.stem: Why must a shoot be cut under water when setting up a potometer?
choices: To keep the leaves hydrated
To prevent air from entering the xylem vessels — an air bubble would break the continuous water column and stop water uptake
To make the stem softer and easier to insert
To remove dirt from the stem
questions.explanation: If the stem is cut in air, air enters the xylem, breaking the water column. Once broken, cohesion is lost and water cannot be pulled up. Cutting under water ensures the xylem remains filled with water.

questions.stem: In spring, where is sucrose translocated FROM and TO in a potato plant?
choices: FROM leaves TO the potato tuber for storage
FROM the potato tuber (stored starch converted to sucrose) TO growing shoots above ground
FROM roots TO leaves
FROM flowers TO roots
questions.explanation: In spring, the potato tuber is a source — stored starch is broken down into sucrose and translocated up through phloem to the developing shoots (sinks) for growth, before the plant has leaves to photosynthesise.

questions.stem: A plant in high humidity shows reduced transpiration. Why?
choices: Stomata close completely in humid conditions
The water vapour concentration gradient between the leaf interior and the outside air is shallow — less diffusion occurs
Humidity damages the leaf cuticle
High humidity prevents photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Transpiration relies on a steep concentration gradient. Moist air outside means the difference in water vapour concentration between inside and outside the leaf is small, so diffusion of water vapour outward slows down.

questions.stem: Which feature is an adaptation of a xerophyte (plant adapted to dry conditions)?
choices: Large, thin leaves for maximum photosynthesis
Sunken stomata in pits — trapping a layer of humid air that reduces the water vapour gradient and slows transpiration
No cuticle — to allow maximum water absorption from air
Stomata on the upper surface only
questions.explanation: Sunken stomata are recessed into the leaf surface in pits. The still, humid air trapped in the pit reduces the concentration gradient, slowing water loss. This is common in pine needles and many desert plants.

questions.stem: What is the role of companion cells in phloem?
choices: They transport water and minerals
They provide ATP energy (from their many mitochondria) to actively load sugars into sieve tube elements at the source
They produce new phloem cells
They form the outer bark of trees
questions.explanation: Sieve tube elements lack a nucleus and most organelles. Companion cells (which retain full cellular machinery) supply ATP to power the active transport of sucrose into sieve tubes and maintain the metabolic needs of the sieve element.

questions.stem: A student investigates transpiration using a potometer. They place a fan blowing over the shoot. What happens to the air bubble movement?
choices: It slows down because the fan cools the leaf
It speeds up — wind removes the humid boundary layer around stomata, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient for faster transpiration
No change — wind does not affect transpiration
It stops because stomata close in response to wind
questions.explanation: Moving air sweeps away the water vapour that accumulates near the stomata, maintaining a steep gradient. This increases the rate of diffusion of water vapour out of the leaf, increasing the transpiration rate.

questions.stem: What substance makes xylem walls waterproof and rigid?
choices: Cellulose
Chitin
Lignin
Starch
questions.explanation: Lignin is deposited in xylem cell walls in rings, spirals, or solid patterns. It is waterproof (prevents water loss from xylem) and extremely rigid (prevents collapse under tension). Wood is essentially lignified xylem.

questions.stem: Why does a plant wilt when it loses too much water?
choices: The plant cells die from dehydration
Vacuoles lose water → cells lose turgor pressure → cells become flaccid → non-woody stems and leaves can no longer stay upright
The xylem vessels collapse
Photosynthesis stops completely
questions.explanation: Plant cells rely on turgor pressure (water pushing against the cell wall) to stay rigid. When water is lost and vacuoles shrink, cells become flaccid and the plant wilts. Watering restores turgor — the plant recovers.

questions.stem: Which mineral deficiency most directly affects the plant's ability to transport sugars in phloem?
choices: Nitrate deficiency — affects protein synthesis
Magnesium deficiency — affects chlorophyll production

None — phloem transport depends on ATP from respiration, which requires glucose from photosynthesis. A deficiency in any essential mineral could indirectly affect it, but phloem itself does not require a specific mineral to function
Potassium deficiency — directly stops phloem flow
questions.explanation: Phloem structure and function do not depend on a single mineral. However, because translocation requires ATP, any mineral deficiency severe enough to impair respiration or photosynthesis would indirectly reduce transport. There is no single 'phloem-specific' mineral.
